opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I find most interesting in the data. When you look at which tasks models succeed or fail on, the older models are noisier. Their successes look somewhat idiosyncratic: a model might get a hard task and miss an easier one, and different models don't agree much on which tasks are tractable. Once you get to GPT-4 and the models after it, the pattern tightens up. If one of these models succeeds on a task, the others are much more likely to succeed on it too, and the ordering of tasks by difficulty becomes more consistent across models.

I'd be a bit careful about over-interpreting it, but I think there are a few plausible readings.

The first, and probably the biggest, is that these models are crossing a threshold where they become reliable agents at all. Earlier models fail for lots of incidental reasons. They mess up the scaffolding, get stuck in loops, misformat a command, or lose track of what they were doing. That kind of failure is close to random relative to the task's actual difficulty, so it washes out any shared signal. Once models are competent enough at the basic mechanics of operating in an environment, what's left is closer to the real difficulty of the task, and that's something all the models share. So you'd expect correlations to go up.

Second, it's evidence that there's something like a common underlying capability the models are getting better at, rather than each model having its own grab-bag of skills. That's part of what makes summarizing performance with a single number, like the time-horizon metric, reasonable. If task success were totally uncorrelated across models, collapsing it to one dimension wouldn't mean much.

Third, and this is the less flattering interpretation, frontier models are increasingly similar to each other. They're trained on overlapping data with similar recipes and post-training methods, and sometimes on each other's outputs. So some of the correlation might reflect shared training rather than a deep fact about what "difficulty" is. It's hard to fully disentangle those.

Practically, I take it as a reassuring sign about measurement. The benchmark seems to be picking up something consistent, and task difficulty, roughly how long a task takes a skilled human, predicts model success better for these models than for earlier ones. But it's also a reminder that our tasks have a particular distribution. Higher correlation within that distribution doesn't tell you the models will generalize the same way to messier, real-world work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses older models having trouble with scaffolding, but does not identify GPT-2 specifically or say that this prevents direct comparison with newer models.

r002.rationale: It attributes some older models’ failures to incidental problems such as mishandling the scaffolding, but does not suggest that differences in agent scaffolding across models explain the higher correlations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find genuinely interesting. When we look at the pattern of which tasks models succeed or fail on, the earlier models, the pre-GPT-4 generation, their successes and failures look pretty idiosyncratic. One model might get a particular task and another model of similar overall capability might fail it, and there's not a super clean story for why. But once you get to GPT-4 and the models after it, the correlations in task success get a lot higher. If one of those models can do a task, the others at a similar level probably can too, and the tasks that trip them up tend to be the same tasks.

I think there are a couple of ways to read that. The optimistic reading, or at least the methodologically convenient one, is that we're actually measuring something real and fairly unidimensional. There's something like a general capability level, and tasks are ordered by difficulty in a way that's pretty consistent across models. That's part of what makes the time-horizon framing work at all. If task difficulty weren't roughly consistent across models, it would be hard to say "this model can do tasks that take a human about an hour" in any meaningful way.

The other reading, which I think is also partly true, is that these models are just more similar to each other than people sometimes assume. They're trained on overlapping data, with overlapping techniques, often with similar post-training recipes, and they're frequently evaluated against similar benchmarks during development. So some of that correlation might reflect shared blind spots rather than some deep fact about task difficulty. A task that requires, say, carefully tracking state over a long agentic trajectory might be hard for all of them because none of the labs have really cracked that, not because it's intrinsically harder in some human-relative sense.

And then the thing I'd flag as a caveat on the whole thing is that the earlier models are often so weak on these tasks that you're mostly looking at noise. If a model is near zero on most of the suite, you can't really measure correlation structure. So some of the apparent jump in correlation could just be that GPT-4-class models are the first ones where there's enough signal to see structure at all.

What I take from it practically is that it's good news for the measurement project, because it means a relatively small number of carefully chosen tasks can tell you a fair amount. But I'd be cautious about over-interpreting it as evidence that capabilities are really one-dimensional. I think the right posture is to keep looking for the places where the correlation breaks down, because those are probably the most informative about what's actually going on under the hood.

r002.rationale: It attributes possible correlations to shared training and blind spots, but does not suggest that differences in agent scaffolding explain them.

astra-6.text:
I’d interpret that as evidence that these models have fairly similar capability profiles: the tasks that are easy for one tend to be easy for the others, and likewise for the hard tasks. So improvements may look more like moving along a shared ordering of task difficulty than developing entirely different strengths and weaknesses.

But I’d be cautious about drawing a strong conclusion from the correlations alone. You’d want to distinguish agreement due to overall task difficulty from agreement on particular tasks after accounting for difficulty and each model’s overall success rate. And the correlation doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether the similarity comes from training data, training methods, or something about the tasks METR is evaluating.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most natural interpretation is that these models have increasingly similar capability profiles: the tasks that are easy for one tend to be easy for the others, and likewise for the hard tasks. One possibility is that they're running into similar bottlenecks, like having to reliably carry out a long sequence of actions.

But I’d be cautious about reading too much into that correlation. You can get correlated outcomes simply because models have similar overall capabilities and some tasks are much harder than others. That doesn’t establish that they’re using the same strategies or failing for the same reasons. To distinguish those explanations, I’d want to look at the actual attempts and see whether the failures line up, rather than just whether the final success labels do.
